title: The Brandenburg Gate, Before and After - Quick Summary
items: **The Brandenburg Gate was built in 1788 to 1791** by Carl Gotthard Langhans as a grand city gate on the model of the entrance to the Athens Acropolis. It is the last of Berlin's old city gates still standing, and the Quadriga on top faces east, into the city.

**Napoleon took the Quadriga to Paris as a war trophy in 1806.** Prussia got it back in 1814 and added an iron cross and a Prussian eagle to the goddess's staff, turning her into a victory figure. That is the version you see today.

**After 1945 the Gate remained one of the few recognisable structures** in a Pariser Platz reduced to rubble. It was badly damaged, one horse of the Quadriga survived as a single head, and East and West Berlin jointly restored it in 1956 to 1958.

**From 1961 to 1989 the Gate stood locked inside the death strip** behind the Berlin Wall, closed to everyone. It reopened on 22 December 1989, a few weeks after the Wall fell, and became the symbol of a reunited Germany.

**Today it is a free, open public square you can visit any time.** Look for the patched shrapnel scars on the columns, the double cobblestone line that marks where the Wall ran, and the quiet Room of Silence inside the northern gatehouse.

**Getting there:** Brandenburger Tor station sits right underneath, served by the S-Bahn and the U5. The Gate is the western end of Unter den Linden, a short walk from Museum Island; it is a sight I send guests to, not where my tour begins.
